props.title: Still Walking
props.initialSlug: Family confronts unspoken grief during annual reunion

sections.content: Still Walking represents Japanese director Hirokazu Kore-eda at his most intimate and masterful. Like Yasujirō Ozu's Tokyo Story (1953), it captures the subtle tensions and unspoken emotions of a family gathering over 24 hours. The film's power lies in its patient observation of small moments - the preparation of corn tempura, awkward silences at the dinner table, and fleeting glances between family members still processing a decades-old tragedy. Kore-eda's approach builds on Japan's rich tradition of "home drama" films while bringing his own contemporary sensibility.

sections.content: The film connects deeply to other contemporary Japanese family dramas that explore intergenerational relationships and unresolved grief. Nobody Knows (2004) and Shoplifters (2018), also by Kore-eda, examine different types of families but share his careful attention to domestic rituals and unstated feelings. After Life (1998) demonstrates his early interest in memory and how we process loss, themes that reach their zenith in Still Walking's delicate portrayal of a family's annual memorial gathering.

Still Walking's influence can be seen in later intimate family dramas like Poetry (2010) by Lee Chang-dong and A Separation (2011) by Asghar Farhadi. These films share its ability to mine profound emotional depths from seemingly ordinary family interactions. The careful pacing and attention to domestic detail also echo in works like Our Little Sister (2015), showing how Kore-eda's style has helped shape contemporary Asian cinema's approach to family narratives. sections.content: While Still Walking draws from Japanese cinema's rich tradition of family stories, it also points toward new ways of examining contemporary family dynamics. Films like After the Storm (2016) and The Truth (2019) continue Kore-eda's exploration of family bonds under modern pressures. The influence extends beyond Japan, visible in works like The Farewell (2019) and Minari (2020), which similarly examine cultural traditions and family obligations in changing times.
